entities.name: Mirai
entities.description: Linux-targeting IoT malware that recruits vulnerable devices into a remotely controlled botnet used in DDoS attacks.

architecture_patterns.name: Mirai botnet lifecycle (conceptual)
architecture_patterns.description: High-level lifecycle from exposed device discovery through compromise, reporting, C2 tasking, DDoS participation, and defender containment.
steps: Internet-exposed or reachable IoT asset has a weakness
Malware discovers a potentially vulnerable device
Weak credentials or an exploitable software flaw permits unauthorized access
Compromised device is recruited into the botnet
Botnet infrastructure coordinates activity
Bots generate distributed traffic against a target
Defenders detect, contain, remediate, and recover
security_notes: Conceptual model only; not an operational attack recipe.
Break the chain through secure defaults, patching, management-plane isolation, monitoring, and upstream DDoS controls.

architecture_patterns.name: IoT device hardening baseline
architecture_patterns.description: Reduce the likelihood that an embedded device can be recruited into a botnet.
steps: Inventory device models, firmware, owners, and exposure
Replace default credentials with unique credentials
Disable unnecessary remote administration and Telnet
Install supported firmware updates
Restrict management access to trusted networks
Segment IoT devices and monitor outbound behavior
Replace devices that cannot be supported securely
security_notes: A reboot or factory reset alone is not durable remediation if defaults and vulnerabilities remain.

architecture_patterns.name: Layered DDoS resilience
architecture_patterns.description: Combine application, edge, network-provider, and incident-response measures.
steps: Baseline normal traffic and service health
Detect abnormal volume, protocol patterns, and application pressure
Engage provider or scrubbing services for upstream traffic
Use CDN/Anycast and rate limits where appropriate
Preserve allowlisted legitimate traffic and critical functions
Communicate status and review telemetry after mitigation
security_notes: No single control prevents every DDoS class; controls should be layered and rehearsed.

architecture_patterns.name: Variant and threat-intelligence workflow
architecture_patterns.description: Track the Mirai-derived ecosystem without assuming every family has identical behavior.
steps: Collect samples and telemetry lawfully
Record observed behavior, timestamps, confidence, and provenance
Map variant lineage while distinguishing confirmed from suspected links
Translate indicators into defensive detections and patch priorities
Reassess detections as variants change
security_notes: The source article mixes reported, suspected, and attributed claims; preserve uncertainty.

architecture_patterns.name: Response to a suspected infected IoT device
architecture_patterns.description: A defensive containment and recovery workflow for suspected Mirai infection.
steps: Confirm symptoms with logs and network telemetry
Isolate the device from external access and outbound abuse
Preserve relevant evidence when required
Update firmware or restore a trusted image
Change all default and exposed credentials
Disable unnecessary services and restrict management access
Validate traffic and monitor for reinfection
Retire unsupported equipment
security_notes: Coordinate with the ISP, vendor, and incident-response team when service disruption or widespread compromise is suspected.

architecture_patterns.name: Public malware code reuse and variant evolution
architecture_patterns.description: Public release of malware source can lower the barrier to derivative variants and new targeting.
steps: A codebase becomes publicly available
Other actors reuse or modify it
Variants add target architectures, exploits, or capabilities
Defenders update asset coverage and detection
Patching and secure configuration reduce exploitable surface
security_notes: The same release can aid analysis while also enabling harmful reuse; analysis should remain defensive and authorized.

architecture_patterns.name: Evidence-based incident attribution
architecture_patterns.description: Distinguish technical observations from claims about people or organizations.
steps: Collect verifiable logs and forensic evidence
Correlate infrastructure, samples, timelines, and victim reports
State confidence and alternative hypotheses
Refer legal conclusions to competent authorities
Update assessments when new evidence appears
security_notes: An alias, public claim, or shared codebase alone does not prove authorship or operational control.

derived_rules.rule: Never leave factory-default credentials enabled on Internet-reachable IoT devices.
Disable Telnet and other unnecessary cleartext remote administration services.
Expose device administration only to explicitly trusted management networks.
Track and apply vendor firmware updates for supported devices.
Replace unsupported devices that cannot be secured to an acceptable standard.
Place IoT devices in appropriately restricted network segments.
Monitor and restrict unnecessary outbound connections from embedded devices.
Maintain an inventory of device models, firmware, owners, and exposure.
Do not treat rebooting as full remediation when the original weakness remains.
After factory reset, patch the device and change credentials before reconnecting it.
Alert on unusual outbound volume, unexpected remote access, and abnormal device resource use.
Use layered DDoS protection across application, edge, network, and provider boundaries.
Prepare provider escalation and scrubbing procedures before a major DDoS incident.
Use suitable rate limits and service-level protection without blocking legitimate clients indiscriminately.
Preserve logs and relevant telemetry during incident response where lawful and feasible.
Isolate suspected compromised IoT assets when needed to stop further abuse.
Verify clean firmware, credential changes, and expected traffic before restoring network access.
Record whether a variant, incident, or attribution is confirmed, reported, or suspected.
Keep source provenance and publication dates attached to threat-intelligence claims.
Perform malware analysis and security testing only in authorized, isolated environments.
Do not reuse device passwords across deployments or device fleets.
Track vendor support and end-of-life dates for deployed IoT hardware.
Use vetted indicators and behavior-based detections; do not rely on static indicators alone.
Assume Mirai-derived variants may change targets and capabilities; refresh controls as evidence changes.
Disable unnecessary services and interfaces on IoT and embedded devices.

Monitor unexpected outbound traffic

Conduct a post-incident review

Prioritize default credentials and known exploitable vulnerabilities
Remediate, isolate, or retire high-risk devices
Recheck exposure after changes
